question: Check the entry's oracle-bone language, divination and royal-ancestor coupling using an inscription/corpus or scholarly passage; do not turn one archive's genre into all Shang speech or belief.
protocol: Round-8 freshness recheck: live retrieval on 2026-10-17 of the entry-cited source and independent sources for each prior limit. Every retrieval records exact URL, HTTP status, exact command form, accessed-at date, quoted passage with named location, source kind and passage-support scope. Access failures record the attempted command and status. Passage support is kept separate from whole-claim support; the raw round-6 worker label is preserved untouched and no promotion is claimed.
quote_conventions: Quotes reproduce the retrieved page text with whitespace normalized to single spaces (HTML extraction sometimes leaves a space before punctuation; that is rendered as normal punctuation). Typographic characters (curly quotes, en dashes, printed ellipsis) are kept where the source uses them. Omissions inside a quote are marked [...]; trailing inline reference markers or figure pointers at a quote's end (e.g. superscript citation numbers) are dropped without a marker. Each quote names its location in the same record.

quotes: The inscriptions give us a highly selective record of some of the concerns and events that were relevant to the elite class of the Shang kingdom.

Through such divinations, the Shang hoped to discover the causes of events, the will of their ancestors and of their highest deity, Di, and the correct course of action to take when faced with difficult decisions.
Discovered and translated beginning only in 1899, these oracle bones are the earliest written records of Chinese civilization.
However, the only such Shang dynasty oracle bones discovered have been from the reigns of Wu Ding (r.1198-1189 BCE) and his successors.
A hot bronze rod was applied, producing cracks, which were interpreted as answers to questions (often expressed as a pair of two possible outcomes) that the king and/or his diviner had posed.
Crack-making on yiwei (day 32), Gu divined: "Father Yi (the twentieth Shang king, Xiao Yi, the father of Wu Ding) is harming the king." (excerpt inscription no. 8)

retrievals.source_kind: peer-reviewed (Wang et al., 'An open dataset for oracle bone character recognition and decipherment', Scientific Data 11:976, 2024, doi:10.1038/s41597-024-03807-x)
retrievals.role: peer-reviewed independent leg for corpus status, decipherment limit and physical provenance
quotes: Oracle bone script, one of the earliest known forms of ancient Chinese writing, presents invaluable research materials for scholars studying the humanities and geography of the Shang Dynasty, dating back 3,000 years. (Abstract)
Oracle bone script, etched onto turtle shells and animal bones, stands as one of the earliest forms of writing discovered in China (see Fig. 1). (Background & Summary)
The content encompasses a range of topics including astrology, meteorology, animal husbandry, religion, and ritual practices. (Background & Summary)

Of the 160,000 pieces unearthed, they reveal more than 4,600 distinct OBCs, yet only about a thousand of these have been deciphered, with their meanings and corresponding modern Chinese characters confirmed. (Background & Summary)

They were all unearthed at the Huayuanzhuang East in Yinxu, China, and are currently housed at the Anyang workstation of the Institute of Archaeology, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. These oracle bones date back to the reign of King Wu Ding of the Shang Dynasty. (Fig. 1 caption)
supports_legs: L1 corpus superlative (weaker form: 'one of the earliest known forms')
L5 decipherment limit (~1,000 of >4,600 confirmed)

retrievals.note: Peer-reviewed source; 'one of the earliest' is weaker than the entry's superlative, so it corroborates the direction but not the exclusive ranking.
